name: Freya Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company with a bachelor's degree. I maintain the display software on small boats, and I like finding why a warning vanished from a wet screen before someone takes the vessel out again. I use AI daily to draft tests, but the crew's notes still decide whether a fix is ready. My partner teaches primary school, and we have two children at school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the assistant is good for drafting tests, but it cannot see a wet chart display on a boat. I use AI every day to list cases for our navigation software, then run them against actual device logs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays modest, our household is secure. I earn well as an experienced developer, my partner teaches primary school on regular hours, we have around eleven months of expenses saved, and plenty of tech firms are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the harbour display after every release and compare its position logs with the crew's notes. In the first year we'd add 220 to savings each month while both wages hold, and I'd keep AI on sample voyages without crew names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I want to use a tool that saves time, then spend that time on the cases that made a skipper turn around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fault escaped a normal log check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wet-screen fault hid a shallow-water warning last spring. The log looked normal until I lined it up with the crew note about a flickering display.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What safety habit do you teach your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children know the family boat is only a small borrowed dinghy, not a business. I tell them equipment gets checked before anyone goes onto the water, however clever the screen is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write code, check routes and answer boat owners, so the firm ought to show how many developers it still needs. I'd volunteer for a trial that counts missed warnings, not only faster releases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experience may keep me in the team, but if the software writes and checks most changes, the firm could cut my hours too. We can search with our savings, yet many nearby employers might be making the same choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a six-week comparison of AI fixes and our own fixes on old wet-screen faults, recording missed warnings and review time. If the trial improves both, I'd learn the new approval process; in the first year we'd delay a planned extension to the house until the firm gives us a staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but interested in the test. I am willing to use the tool; I am not willing to hide a missed shallow-water warning to make the tool look quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should judge the trial besides developers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trial needs the wet-screen case and a crew member's report. If an AI patch passes the log check but the screen still flickers, the crew should get to say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does delaying the extension mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had sketches for the extension, but no builder booked. I'd rather keep the money available for the mortgage if my hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches navigation code before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A boat owner still needs to know who is paid to answer when the display misses shallow water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my development post could go if the cheaper system designs and tests routes itself. Eleven months saved and my partner's teaching wage let us search without losing the house immediately, but I cannot assume other firms will keep hiring coders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd put the wet-screen fix into a safe work record and ask three marine-equipment firms about paid device-testing posts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real openings whose wage with my partner's pay covers mortgage and school costs; if none qualify, I'd search other paid work using savings and ask the lender about hardship terms before a missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I have time to look, but I expect the thing that pays me to change before I can learn a whole new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would boat-device testing be safe when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Device testing on boats would mean handling wet equipment, not only reading logs. Robots may take more hands-on work around 2031, so I would ask firms whether paid people still visit boats before treating that as a long-term refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a new offer real to your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want the offer in writing, with hours and pay. We would not start the house extension on a possible job, even with savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us test which boat checks still need a person holding the device. Robots arrive around 2034, but thinking AI reaches our software first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn field device testing if a firm pays for safe training, though my developer post might shrink before then. I would not turn savings into course fees unless a paid rotation and real supervision came with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for paid time to build a wet-screen replay on retired company equipment, using crew notes and no private voyages, with a named field tester checking my results. I'd take firm-funded marine-safety training only for a paid device-testing rotation that keeps my current wage and names the person supervising me; if no such offer appears, I'd keep developing software and ask other firms about paid testing. If coding ends after 2031, I'd apply only to actual paid openings whose combined household wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the current job, but five years let me test the field path. I would still ask whether firms expect to keep people doing boat visits when robots spread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the wet screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd replay the shallow-water warning on a retired display and compare the flicker with the crew note while the named tester checks my result. I would not operate boat equipment until trained and authorised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a rotation promise on paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask whether the rotation keeps my wage and names the person teaching me. If either answer is missing, I keep the developer job and ask another firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 lets people keep a record of where the screen and the real water disagree. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036, with hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might be in paid device testing or another software job. Our higher wages, my partner's teaching and eleven-month cushion make the next few years secure, but a decade is not proof that any one future role pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wet-screen case log and fix the display problems we find. We'd save 220 monthly while both wages hold, and in the first year after 2036 I'd move only for a signed device-testing or software offer whose combined wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the present. I can keep earning and make a later decision from a real offer, not a guess about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your work log show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The log would show the flickering screen, the crew note and the corrected warning, with private voyage details removed. I want a future employer to see the wet-screen fault I traced, not a copied boat owner's journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about boat work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children ask about working on boats. I'd tell them to seek a paid apprenticeship with a real mentor if they like the work, then check the openings when they are old enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because navigation code could cheapen before I have paid field skills. A notice period, real supervised device-testing places and wages that cover the mortgage would help us choose sensibly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who tells a boat owner that a screen missed shallow water. The developer who signed the release should hear the crew's account before calling the fix complete.

headlineQuote: The developer who signed the release should hear the crew's account before calling the fix complete.
